draft.title: Ideas, issues and points of view
card: An idea or issue is something a text makes readers think about, such as friendship, fairness or belonging. A text shows it through what characters do and what happens to them.
A text rarely states its idea outright. Readers work it out by noticing how characters act, what they want and how events turn out.
The point of view is the position the story is told from. It might be one character's view, or a storyteller outside the events.
The point of view shapes what readers know and feel. A story told by one character shows that character's thoughts, but may leave out how others see things.
draft.remember: Texts show ideas through characters and events, and the point of view shapes what readers see.

a.q: In a story, Jaya shares her lunch with a new student who has no friends yet. Which idea does this event most clearly explore?
opts: Kindness and friendship
Revenge and anger
Fear of the dark
Winning at any cost
a.why: Jaya's action shows care for someone who is alone, so the event explores kindness and friendship. Winning at any cost is tempting only if the story were about competition, but nothing here shows that.
a.clue: Think about what Jaya's action shows about how she treats others.

b.q: A story about a school sports day is told only through Leo, who feels left out after he is picked last for the team. What does this point of view do?
opts: Lets readers feel Leo's hurt but not how the others feel
Shows readers the private thoughts of every character
Proves that the other students were being unfair
Tells readers the story from outside the events only
b.why: Telling the story through Leo lets readers share his thoughts and hurt, while the others' feelings stay hidden. It does not prove the others were unfair, because readers only see Leo's view of what happened.
b.clue: Whose thoughts can readers see, and whose stay hidden?

b.best: Lets readers feel Leo's hurt but not how the others feel

problems.detail: The card says a one-character view 'may leave out how others see things'. The right option ('but not how the others feel') and the why ('the others' feelings stay hidden') make this absolute. Readers can still infer others' feelings from what Leo notices them say and do. Softer wording would fit the card better, such as 'but shows less of how the others feel'.

check.summary: Both questions have one clear right answer. In question b, the right option and its why say other characters' feelings are completely hidden, where the card only says a single narrator may leave them out.
